meta.title: Database Indexing Explained: B+ Trees, Composite & Covering Indexes
meta.subtitle: from full scans to B+ trees and covering indexes

cover.summary: How relational databases use indexes to avoid scanning whole tables: the B+ tree structure, composite and covering indexes, reading query plans, the cost indexes add to writes, and a practical tuning workflow.
cover.big_idea: an index trades write speed for read speed!

sections.title: why indexes exist
sections.subtitle: avoiding the full scan

blocks.text: Without an index the database has only one way to answer a filter: read every row of the table and test it (a sequential scan). Cost grows linearly with table size, so a query that is instant on 10k rows crawls on 100M.
A separate, sorted data structure that maps column values to the location of matching rows, so the engine can jump straight to them.

items: table data lives in unordered pages on disk (the heap)
an index stores (key -> row pointer) pairs in key order
lookups become logarithmic instead of linear
the price: extra disk space and slower writes

blocks.title: find one user
blocks.text: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@b.com' scans millions of rows; with an index on email it touches a handful of pages.

diagram.title: scan vs lookup
diagram.caption: same query, two very different amounts of work

key_takeaways: no index = read every row
an index is a sorted key -> row-pointer map
it speeds reads and taxes writes

recall.q: What does an index change about how a filter query is answered?
recall.a: It replaces a linear scan of every row with a logarithmic lookup in a sorted structure that points to the matching rows.

sections.title: the B+ tree
sections.subtitle: what most indexes really are

blocks.text: Most relational databases build indexes as B+ trees: a balanced tree where internal nodes only route the search and all keys with their row pointers live in the leaf level.

items: start at the root page
compare the search key with the separator keys to pick a child
repeat down the internal levels
land in a leaf and find the key
follow the row pointer into the table

blocks.text: How many children one node holds. Pages are large, so fan-out is in the hundreds and the tree stays very shallow.
height ~ log_fanout(N)
Leaves are linked in order, which is why range scans (BETWEEN, ORDER BY) are cheap: find the start, then walk sideways.

diagram.title: B+ tree lookup
diagram.caption: internal nodes route, leaves hold the keys

key_takeaways: B+ trees stay balanced and shallow
all data pointers sit in linked leaves
range queries walk the leaf chain

recall.q: Why can a billion-row index be searched in only a few page reads?
recall.a: Fan-out is in the hundreds, so tree height is log base fan-out of N, which is just a few levels.

sections.title: reading the query plan
sections.subtitle: EXPLAIN is your microscope

blocks.text: Never guess whether an index is used: ask the planner. EXPLAIN shows the chosen strategy and ANALYZE adds real timings and row counts.

rows: walks the index, then fetches rows from the table
collects many matches first, then reads table pages in order

blocks.text: Compare estimated rows with actual rows; a big gap usually means stale statistics.

diagram.title: life of a query
diagram.caption: the planner decides before anything runs

key_takeaways: use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, do not guess
know Seq / Index / Index Only / Bitmap
estimates vs actuals expose bad statistics

recall.q: How do you check whether a query actually uses your index?
recall.a: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) and look at the scan node type and the estimated versus actual row counts.

sections.title: composite indexes
sections.subtitle: column order matters

blocks.text: An index on several columns is sorted by the first column, then the second within equal firsts, and so on. It helps a query only if the filter uses a leftmost prefix of the columns.

blocks.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at);

blocks.text: Put equality columns first and the range column last; a range on an early column stops the later columns from narrowing the search.

diagram.title: sort order inside the index
diagram.caption: customer_id is the major sort key

key_takeaways: leftmost-prefix rule
equality columns first, range last
one composite index can replace several single ones

recall.q: Why does an index on (a, b) not help a query that filters only on b?
recall.a: It is sorted by a first, so the b values are scattered across the whole index and cannot be binary-searched.

sections.title: covering indexes
sections.subtitle: never touch the table

blocks.text: An index that contains every column the query needs, so the engine returns results from the index alone (an index-only scan).
Normally each match costs an extra random read into the table to fetch the row. A covering index removes that hop.

blocks.title: cover a dashboard query
blocks.text: SELECT status, count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 GROUP BY status can be served entirely by an index on (customer_id, status).

items: extra INCLUDE columns can ride along without being sort keys
wider indexes are bigger and cost more on writes
cover only the hottest queries

key_takeaways: covering = all needed columns live in the index
saves one table read per match
do not over-widen indexes

recall.q: What makes an index covering, and what does it save?
recall.a: It holds every column the query uses, saving the random table read for each matching row.

sections.title: the write tax
sections.subtitle: every index slows INSERT

blocks.text: Each insert, update of an indexed column, or delete must also modify every index on the table. More indexes means more pages written and more locking.

items: insert the row into the table
for each index, find the correct leaf
insert the key into the leaf
if the leaf is full, split it and update the parent
repeat for the next index

blocks.text: When a full leaf page receives a new key it is divided in two; this costs extra I/O and can fragment the index.
A table with 10 indexes does roughly 10 index writes per row inserted.

diagram.title: cost of one insert
diagram.caption: repeated for every index on the table

key_takeaways: writes touch every index
page splits add I/O
index only what queries need

recall.q: Why can adding many indexes make a write-heavy table slower?
recall.a: Every insert or update must also be applied to each index, including leaf lookups and possible page splits.

sections.title: when not to index
sections.subtitle: low value, high cost

items: tiny tables: a sequential scan is already cheap
low-cardinality columns (e.g. a boolean) match too many rows to be selective
columns that are rarely filtered or joined
write-heavy tables where read speed is not critical

blocks.text: The planner will ignore an index if it expects to read a large fraction of the table anyway, because many random index hops cost more than one sequential pass.
A partial index (only the rows that matter) can rescue a skewed boolean column.

diagram.title: selective vs unselective
diagram.caption: selectivity decides the value of an index

key_takeaways: selectivity is what makes an index pay off
skip indexes on tiny or write-heavy tables
partial indexes help skewed data

recall.q: Why might the planner ignore an index on a boolean column?
recall.a: Half the table matches, so many random index hops cost more than one sequential scan.

sections.title: a tuning workflow
sections.subtitle: measure, change, re-measure

items: find the slow query from logs or monitoring
run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on it
form a hypothesis (missing index, wrong column order, stale stats)
create or adjust one index
re-run EXPLAIN and compare timings
drop indexes that no query uses

blocks.text: Change one thing at a time, otherwise you cannot tell which change helped.
Indexes are a living part of the schema: revisit them as query patterns change and remove the unused ones to reclaim write speed and disk.

diagram.title: index strategy over time
diagram.caption: start simple, add only on evidence

key_takeaways: measure before and after
one change at a time
prune unused indexes

recall.q: Describe the loop you follow when tuning a slow query with indexes.
recall.a: Find it, EXPLAIN ANALYZE it, hypothesise, change one index, re-measure, and drop indexes nobody uses.

sections.title: putting it together
sections.subtitle: the index checklist

items: index the columns you filter, join and sort on
order composite columns: equality first, range last
cover the hottest read paths
weigh each index against its write cost
verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE

blocks.text: benefit = reads saved - write cost - storage

diagram.title: the indexing checklist
diagram.caption: what to weigh before adding an index

key_takeaways: indexes trade write speed and space for read speed
always verify with the planner

recall.q: What is the one-sentence rule for deciding whether to add an index?
recall.a: Add it when the reads it saves on selective, frequent queries outweigh the extra write and storage cost, and confirm with EXPLAIN.

glossary.definition: Sorted structure mapping column values to row locations.
Balanced tree with routing nodes above and linked key-bearing leaves.
Number of children per tree node; large fan-out keeps the tree shallow.
Reading every row of a table to test a filter.
Index over several columns, sorted by the first, then the next.
Rule that a composite index helps only if the filter uses its first column(s).
Index containing all columns a query needs, enabling an index-only scan.
How small a fraction of rows a filter matches; high selectivity favours an index.
Dividing a full index page in two when a new key arrives.
Component that chooses the cheapest execution strategy using statistics.

recap.title: the whole picture, recapped
points: an index is a sorted key -> row-pointer map, usually a B+ tree
shallow trees make lookups logarithmic and ranges cheap
EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you what the planner really does
composite order and covering columns decide how much work remains
every index taxes writes and storage, so index selectively and prune
